common_name: Druid Air Plant (Chlorophyll-Form Ionantha, Peach-Blush Tillandsia)

planting.note: Mount on cork bark, driftwood, or shells in bright indirect to gentle morning light rather than potting in soil. Druid needs the same soak-and-dry cycle as the species, but its muted color response means growers should judge bloom timing by the flower spike rather than by a red flush.

directions: This selection of Tillandsia ionantha traces back to a Drew Schulz collection made near Veracruz, Mexico around 1970, and it stands apart from ordinary ionantha by what it fails to do: even at flowering time in strong light, the narrow gray-green leaves stay green and shift only toward soft peach and yellow tones instead of the vivid red blush typical of the species. Its tubular flowers are white rather than the violet seen on most ionantha forms, a trait collectors use to identify it at a glance. Because it lacks the anthocyanin blush, Druid tends to look less dramatic than red-form ionantha in a mixed display, but its pale coloring and clumping habit make it a useful accent among more saturated air plants. Soak by dunking for 20-30 minutes twice weekly in warm months, then shake dry and let it dry fully within a few hours to avoid basal rot.
sources: Bird Rock Tropicals — Tillandsia ionantha 'Druid' cultivar notes

common_name: Cotton Candy Air Plant (Stricta-Recurvifolia Hybrid Tillandsia)

planting.note: Mount on bark or wire, or display loose in a dish, in bright indirect light with strong air movement; this hybrid grows quickly and clumps into offsets faster than either parent species.

directions: Cotton Candy is a hybrid raised by Tillandsia breeder Mark Dimmitt by crossing Tillandsia stricta with Tillandsia recurvifolia, and it inherits a fuller, softer rosette than either parent alone. Numerous thin, silvery, semi-soft leaves build into a rounded 8-inch rosette, and at bloom time a large, semi-pendant spike of bright rose-red bracts emerges, holding the flowers well clear of the foliage for weeks. It is part of the same hybrid grex as the related cultivar 'Houston', though Cotton Candy has noticeably thinner, softer leaves than its sibling. Soak or mist several times a week, favoring more frequent misting in bright, dry indoor spots and less in humid greenhouse conditions, and always allow the rosette to dry within a few hours of watering.
sources: Rainforest Flora — Tillandsia 'Houston Cotton Candy' notes

common_name: Little Harv Bromeliad (Bullis Hybrid Aechmea, Silver-Banded Urn Plant)

planting.note: Grow in a coarse, fast-draining bark mix in a large container or mount on a tree trunk in zone 10-11; despite the small-sounding name this hybrid grows into a substantial landscape specimen, so give it several feet of clearance.

directions: Little Harv is a Bullis Bromeliads hybrid combining the bold silver-gray banding of Aechmea chantinii with the sturdier, more sun-tolerant constitution of a rubens-type parent, and despite its diminutive name it matures into one of the larger landscape aechmeas, with an arching rosette reaching several feet across. Leaf color shifts with light exposure, ranging from bluish-green in shade to a bronzy red-silver blush in brighter conditions, and mature plants send up a tall, branched flower spike in vivid pink topped with small yellow flowers. It is popular in warm-climate landscape plantings and as a large container specimen because it tolerates more direct sun than most chantinii-type hybrids without losing its banded pattern. Keep the central cup topped with water, flush it periodically, and expect the rosette to persist for a couple of years before flowering and producing pups at its base.
sources: Garden.org Plant Files — Aechmea chantinii 'Little Harv'

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in zone 10-11; cannot tolerate frost or sustained temperatures below 55°F. Pot in a well-draining, slightly acidic bark-based mix and keep the central cup filled with water.

directions: Denise is a Deroose-bred Guzmania hybrid selected for the contrast between its green-and-white striped foliage and its glowing reddish-orange inflorescence, giving it visual interest even when out of bloom, unlike many solid-green Guzmania cultivars. The rosette of smooth, arching leaves grows to a medium size and tolerates deep filtered shade or interior light better than most flowering houseplants, making it well suited to offices and low-light rooms. Keep the central cup topped with fresh water and flush it every few weeks to prevent stagnation, and mist occasionally in dry indoor air. Like all Guzmania, the flowering rosette blooms once over several months and then declines, with new pups forming at the base for propagation.
sources: Bromeliad Cultivar Register (Bromeliad Society International) — Guzmania hybrids

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in zone 10-11; cannot tolerate frost or sustained temperatures below 55°F. Pot in a well-draining, slightly acidic bark-based mix and keep the central cup filled with water.

directions: Amaranth is a registered Guzmania hybrid crossing the purple-flushed form of Guzmania wittmackii with Guzmania lingulata, combining the compact habit of its lingulata parent with richer bract coloring inherited from wittmackii. The rosette of glossy, strap-shaped leaves stays modest in size compared to many torch bromeliads, making it a good fit for windowsills and small shaded containers. It shares the deep-shade tolerance typical of Guzmania hybrids, flowering reliably even in interior rooms with only bright indirect light. Keep the central cup filled with fresh water, flush it periodically to avoid stagnation, and separate offset pups once they reach a few inches tall after the parent rosette finishes blooming and begins to decline.
sources: Bromeliad Cultivar Register (Bromeliad Society International) — Guzmania 'Amaranth'

planting.note: Plant outdoors as a groundcover or accent in zone 10-11, or grow in shallow pots elsewhere; give intense filtered light rather than deep shade to develop full leaf color.

directions: Gazpacho is a long-established Neoregelia hybrid of uncertain parentage, generally believed to descend from a cross involving Neoregelia chlorosticta and the popular cultivar 'Fireball', and it produces a flat, spreading rosette patterned in bold blotches of deep red against green rather than a uniform flush of color. The mottled, almost marbled leaf pattern is more variable and painterly than the solid coloring of plainer red-form Neoregelia, giving each rosette a slightly different look. It needs brighter, more intense filtered light than typical shade bromeliads to bring out strong contrast between the red and green zones, fading toward plain green in deep shade. Keep the central cup filled with water, divide crowded clumps every year or two, and expect offsets to root readily beside the parent rosette.
sources: Florida Council of Bromeliad Societies — Neoregelia cultivar guide
